clue.text: In court, long for prestige

indicators.note: the clue opens by placing the yearning word in the court abbreviation, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: to long for something is to ache for it

explanation.surface: Someone at court yearns for status and standing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In court' reads as a setting, but 'In' is the container signal; 'long' is a verb here, not an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: cachet is the distinction or prestige that something confers.

clue.text: American state song about area cut short

indicators.note: about says the song word goes round the shortened area word

parts.note: an aria is a song in an opera

indicators.note: cut short drops the last letter of the area word

parts.note: a zone is an area

explanation.surface: A song about a region of America, cut short.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut short' trims ZONE to ZON, which ARIA goes 'about'.
explanation.definitionFit: Arizona is a south-western US state, home of the Grand Canyon.

clue.text: Virgin eschews top speed

indicators.note: eschews top means the first letter of the word for virgin is shunned

parts.note: a virgin is chaste

explanation.surface: Virgin, the airline or brand, avoids top speed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Virgin' suggests Richard Branson's company, but it is the adjective chaste, losing its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Haste is speed or hurry in doing something.

clue.text: Bill left on slate possibly for seasoning

parts.note: a tab is a bill, as at a bar

indicators.note: possibly says the letters of slate could be arranged another way

explanation.surface: A restaurant bill left on a slate, perhaps for the seasoning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' is the anagram signal for slate; 'on' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Table salt is the fine salt used at meals, the commonest condiment for flavouring food.

clue.text: Al Capone's panic around France, oddly

indicators.note: the panic word is wrapped around the picked letters of France, so it goes outside them

parts.note: to panic someone is to scare them

indicators.note: oddly asks for the letters in the odd-numbered places of France: first, third and fifth

explanation.surface: The gangster Al Capone gets into a panic somewhere around France, oddly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oddly' picks F, A and C from France; 'around' puts SCARE round them. The 's of 'Al Capone's' stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Scarface was the nickname of the Chicago gangster, from the scars on his cheek.

clue.text: Almost certain advantage is more than is needed

indicators.note: almost means the certain word is not quite finished, losing its last letter

parts.note: sure means certain
a plus is an advantage or benefit

explanation.surface: Being almost certain is an advantage that's more than needed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost' cuts SURE to SUR.
explanation.definitionFit: A surplus is an excess, an amount beyond what is required.

clue.text: Fool — crossing motorway must be wrong!

indicators.note: crossing has the fool word straddling the road, which sits inside it

parts.note: an ass is a fool
the M1 is Britain's main north-south motorway, written MI

explanation.surface: A fool walking across a motorway must have something wrong with him.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1 is the motorway from London to Leeds; its digit 1 is read as the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: Amiss means faulty or not as it should be, a synonym of awry.

clue.text: Basset drinking coffee is given praise

indicators.note: drinking says the dog takes the coffee into himself, so it goes inside

parts.note: Fred Basset is a basset hound in a long-running British newspaper comic strip
a latte is a milky coffee

explanation.surface: A basset hound lapping up coffee gets praised by its owner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Basset' looks like the breed, but stands for FRED, from the British cartoon dog Fred Basset.
explanation.definitionFit: To be flattered is to receive compliments, often excessive, a form of being lauded.

clue.text: Church getting over new name and indication of rank

indicators.note: new says the letters of over are made into a fresh arrangement

explanation.surface: A church takes over a new name, bestowing a mark of rank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new' rearranges OVER to EVRO; 'getting' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A chevron is the V-shaped stripe on a uniform sleeve that shows a soldier's rank.

clue.text: Disobedient in playing outside barn

indicators.note: playing suggests the letters of outside and barn are toyed with and rearranged together

explanation.surface: A disobedient child is playing outside the barn instead of doing chores.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' stays as written at the front; 'playing' rearranges OUTSIDE and BARN into SUBORDINATE, a neat hidden irony.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: an insubordinate person refuses to obey those in authority.

clue.text: Fertiliser coming as a result of dog's dinner?

definitions.meaning: a garden fertiliser made from ground animal bones
read literally, a meal of a bone, which is what a dog would eat; the question mark flags the playful reading

explanation.surface: Garden fertiliser turns out to be the result of feeding the dog.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dog's dinner' is a British idiom for a mess, but here it is read literally as a meal of a bone.
explanation.definitionFit: Ground animal bones are a common garden fertiliser rich in phosphorus, sold under this name.

clue.text: St Andrew's cross, left out — that's supposed to be funny

indicators.note: out says the letter for left is dropped from the heraldic cross word

parts.note: St Andrew's cross is the X-shaped saltire on Scotland's flag

explanation.surface: Someone cross on St Andrew's Day has been left out of a joke.
explanation.walkthrough: The saltire is the diagonal white cross on blue of the Scottish flag; Andrew is Scotland's patron saint.
explanation.definitionFit: Satire is comic writing or performance that mocks its targets, so it is meant to amuse.

clue.text: Fliers fail, possibly, lacking the ultimate in moral fibre

parts.note: the RAF, Britain's Royal Air Force, is a body of fliers

indicators.note: possibly says the remaining letters of fail could be arranged another way
lacking says the chosen letter goes missing from the word fail
the ultimate in picks the final letter of moral

explanation.surface: Pilots who fail may lack the moral fibre needed to fly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lacking the ultimate in moral' removes L from FAIL, leaving FAI, which 'possibly' rearranges to FIA. 'Moral fibre' is a set phrase that hides the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Raffia is a natural fibre from palm leaves used for weaving and tying.

clue.text: Two original elements in schnapps, perhaps

parts.note: fire is one of the four classical elements of ancient philosophy
water is another of the four classical elements

explanation.surface: Schnapps is perhaps made from two basic ingredients.
explanation.walkthrough: The ancient elements were earth, air, fire and water; 'perhaps' marks schnapps as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Firewater is slang for strong spirits, and schnapps is one such spirit.

clue.text: Carol's about to tolerate bad language

indicators.note: about says the singing word goes round the tolerating word

parts.note: to carol is to sing; the 's stands for is
to wear something can mean to accept or put up with it

explanation.surface: Carol is about to put up with someone's foul language.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carol' looks like a woman's name but is the verb to sing; 'about' is the container signal, not 'about to'.
explanation.definitionFit: Swearing is the use of oaths and obscenities, a synonym for foul talk.

clue.text: With flag raised, make a speech and disappear

indicators.note: raised in a down clue means the paving word reads upwards, bottom to top

parts.note: a flag is a paving stone, so to flag is to pave
to orate is to make a speech

explanation.surface: A speaker raises a flag, gives an address and then vanishes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flag' looks like a banner, but is a flagstone, so PAVE; 'raised' turns it to EVAP.
explanation.definitionFit: To evaporate is to turn into vapour, or figuratively to vanish.

clue.text: Fire it off after a quiet drink

indicators.note: after says the rearranged letters follow the article and the quiet letter

parts.note: P, for piano, is the musical mark for quiet

indicators.note: off suggests the letters of fire and it have gone off, out of order

explanation.surface: An order to fire off a gun after a moment's quiet, with a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' is the anagram signal for 'Fire it'; 'after' places that rearrangement behind the article and the quiet letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An aperitif is an alcoholic drink taken before a meal to stimulate the appetite.

clue.text: Punter's beginning on beer, beer and beer

indicators.note: on in a down clue puts the picked letter on top of what follows
beginning picks out the first letter of the punter's word

parts.note: ale is a kind of beer
ale again, a second helping of beer

explanation.surface: A drinker starts on beer, then more beer, then more beer.
explanation.walkthrough: The first two 'beer's each give ALE; the third is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Pale ale is a light-coloured bitter beer brewed from pale malt.

clue.text: Story resulting from conflict with no end to war

indicators.note: with no says the chosen letter is taken away from the conflict word

parts.note: friction is conflict or discord

indicators.note: end to picks the last letter of war

explanation.surface: A tale emerges from a conflict where war never ends.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no end to war' removes R from FRICTION.
explanation.definitionFit: Fiction is invented narrative, a made-up tale.

clue.text: Checks test initially adopted by German cars

indicators.note: adopted by says the picked letter is taken into the car word

parts.note: Audi is a German car maker, so its cars are Audis

indicators.note: initially picks the first letter of test

explanation.surface: German cars go through checks and initial tests before sale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initially' takes T from test; 'adopted by' puts it inside AUDIS.
explanation.definitionFit: Audits are formal inspections or examinations, especially of financial accounts.

clue.text: Catch up with African organisation youth leader's right to occupation

indicators.note: up in a down clue means the catching word reads from bottom to top

parts.note: to net is to catch
the ANC is the African National Congress of South Africa

indicators.note: leader's picks the first letter of youth

explanation.surface: Catching up with an African body's youth leader about a claim to land.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns NET to TEN. The 's of 'leader's' is 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A tenancy is the legal right to occupy land or property as a tenant.

clue.text: Burst balloon

definitions.meaning: an outburst or explosion, as of anger
to inflate or swell, or to enlarge a photograph

explanation.definitionFit: A blow-up is an explosion or angry outburst, and to blow up is to inflate or enlarge.

clue.text: Lay down and drink

definitions.meaning: to set something down heavily or carelessly

explanation.definitionFit: To plonk is to put down with a thud, and plonk is British slang for cheap wine.

clue.text: Dutch shoe protecting flimsy socks, say

indicators.note: protecting says the shoe word surrounds and shields the flimsy word

parts.note: a clog is the wooden shoe associated with the Netherlands
flimsy means thin and insubstantial

explanation.surface: A Dutch clog protects feet that only have flimsy socks on them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'socks, say' marks socks as one example of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Socks are an example of garments, things worn on the body.

clue.text: Hard, when accepting the Italian's salutes

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

indicators.note: accepting says the when word takes the Italian article into itself

parts.note: as can mean when, as in 'as I left'
il is Italian for the; the 's is a possessive link

explanation.surface: It's hard when one has to accept an Italian's greetings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'accepting' is the container signal; 'the Italian' means the Italian word for 'the'.
explanation.definitionFit: To hail someone is to greet or salute them, so hails are salutes.

clue.text: Tyrannical writer from Italy changing sides halfway through

parts.note: an author is a writer

indicators.note: changing sides means left becomes right, here in the middle of the national word

parts.note: something from Italy is Italian; from is the link
L stands for left, one of the two sides
R stands for right, the other side

explanation.surface: An Italian writer of tyrannical views switches political sides partway through.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changing sides halfway through' swaps the L (left) in the middle of ITALIAN for R (right), giving ITARIAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Authoritarian means enforcing strict obedience to authority, a near-synonym of despotic.

clue.text: Hide from animal, wielding sabre in front of family

indicators.note: in front of says the rearranged letters come before the family word
wielding suggests the sabre is swung about, scrambling its letters

parts.note: kin means family or relatives

explanation.surface: Someone hides from an animal while wielding a sabre before their family.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wielding' rearranges SABRE to BEARS; 'Hide' looks like a verb but is a noun, an animal's skin.
explanation.definitionFit: A bearskin is the pelt of a bear, the hide taken from that animal.

clue.text: Has a go at literary compositions

definitions.meaning: attempts or tries, the verb sense
short written pieces on a subject

explanation.definitionFit: To essay something is to attempt it, and essays are also short prose pieces.
